newsitem.title: USA: Royal Bank Canada seeks U.S. acquisition.
newsitem.headline: Royal Bank Canada seeks U.S. acquisition.

text.p: Royal Bank of Canada Vice Chairman Bruce Galloway said the bank is looking to acquire a wealth management company in the United States and expand its other businesses south of the border.

"We see great opportunities to expand our wealth management business," he told the New England-Canada Business Council luncheon in Boston. "We will probably grow in the wealth management area through a series of acquisitions in different parts of the business."
However, Galloway said he did not expect the bank to make any major announcements during the year.
"I don't think you'll see a big splash in 1997," he said.

Galloway said he expected Royal Bank to build on its current derivatives and asset securitization business in the United States and to push into the syndicated lending, trading and structured finance businesses.
He did not expect the Royal Bank or any of the other major Canadian banks, besides the Bank of Montreal, to compete in the traditional retail banking area in the United States.

"The future for Canadian banks in the United States is not going to be a bricks and morter game," he said. "Few foreign banks have the appetite or the deep pockets that are required to take on the banks in the retail area."
One of those few banks is Bank of Montreal, which bought Harris Bankcorp in the 1980s, he noted.

Canadian banks have several advantages over their American counterparts, he said. Canadian banks are experienced at offering a variety of services and owning companies with different cultures, he said. They also are leaner and have strong debt ratings, he said.

While looking south, Galloway said Canadian banks will face increasing competition at home from U.S. banks and trusts, U.S. investment dealers and non-bank competitors. That has created excess capacity and liquidity and spreads in traditional banking to narrow, while credit demand has slackened.
Meanwhile, Schedule Two banks, many owned by foreign banks, are getting broader powers, he said.

"Ultimately one can see the possibility of an American bank making major inroads using more efficient delivery systems than our traditional branch network, and with a change of regulations, possibly making a major acquisition as well," he said.
Federal laws currently prevent mergers by limiting investors to a maximum 10 percent stake in a Canadian bank.
"It's not surprising that Canadian bankers are increasingly raising the prospects of merging with each other," he said.
